scenes.visual: THE WORLD, kept for both chapters (16:9, dark navy background). COLOUR BY CLASS, same in every scene: round yellow seeds GOLD; round green GREEN; wrinkled yellow ORANGE; wrinkled green TEAL. Expected counts are WHITE dashed 'ghost' lines; probabilities are WHITE text on branches; anything made by chance in a simulation is drawn in pale GREY first and takes its class colour when it settles. Chromosomes are BLUE rods. Numbers and fractions always appear on screen as text, never only spoken. Title card 'How Far Is Too Far?' fades in over chapter 1's four ghost lines and their faint clouds of grey ticks.

scenes.tts: How far can counts stray from a ratio before chance becomes a poor explanation? Chapter one showed that real counts usually scatter. Now we measure the scatter.
scenes.caption: How far can counts stray from a ratio before chance becomes a poor explanation? Chapter 1 showed that real counts usually scatter. Now we measure the scatter.
scenes.visual: Title fades. The four class bars return (GOLD, GREEN, ORANGE, TEAL) with their WHITE ghost lines. A ruler icon slides in from the right and hovers over the bars.
scenes.narration: How far can counts stray from a ratio before chance becomes a poor explanation? Chapter 1 showed that real counts usually scatter. Now we measure the scatter.

scenes.tts: Back to Mendel's seeds. Every class missed its predicted count by a few seeds. Some came in high, and some came in low. Is that close enough to keep the ratio?
scenes.caption: Back to Mendel's seeds. Every class missed its predicted count by a few seeds. Some came in high, and some came in low. Is that close enough to keep the ratio?
scenes.visual: Mendel's bars 315, 108, 101, 32 against ghost lines 312.75, 104.25, 104.25, 34.75. The gap of each bar is drawn as a short arrow with its value on screen: +2.25, +3.75, −3.25, −2.75. Upward arrows WHITE, downward arrows pale GREY.
scenes.narration: Back to Mendel's seeds. Every class missed its predicted count by a few seeds. Some came in high, and some came in low. Is that close enough to keep the ratio?

scenes.tts: Is a miss of a few seeds a lot? That depends on the class. In this cross, chance moves a bigger pile further than a smaller one. The round yellow pile, the biggest, strays furthest. The small wrinkled green pile strays least. So judge each miss against the scatter in its own class.
scenes.visual: Around each ghost line a pale whisker grows showing chance's typical miss, with its value on screen: 11.7, 9.2, 9.2, 5.7 seeds (computed: the square root of 556 × p × (1 − p)). The GOLD whisker is clearly the widest, the TEAL one the narrowest. Each of Mendel's arrows sits well inside its whisker.
scenes.narration: Is a miss of a few seeds a lot? That depends on the class. In this cross, chance moves a bigger pile further than a smaller one. The round yellow pile, the biggest, strays furthest. The small wrinkled green pile strays least. So judge each miss against the scatter in its own class.

scenes.tts: Karl Pearson built a score for this. For each class, square the miss, so high and low both count. Divide by the expected count. That roughly puts each miss on its own class's scale. Then add the classes.
scenes.caption: Karl Pearson built a score for this. For each class, square the miss, so high and low both count. Divide by the expected count. That roughly puts each miss on its own class's scale. Then add the classes.
scenes.visual: A portrait-free text tag 'Karl Pearson, 1900'. The formula builds term by term at the top: '(O − E)²' when 'square', then '/ E' when 'divide', then 'Σ' in front when 'add'. Below it, the four terms for Mendel's classes appear silently in their class colours (0.016, 0.135, 0.101, 0.218), then a plus sign joins them.
scenes.narration: Karl Pearson built a score for this. For each class, square the miss, so high and low both count. Divide by the expected count. That roughly puts each miss on its own class's scale. Then add the classes.

scenes.tts: The score is called kai-square. Zero means a perfect match, and bigger means further off. Mendel's seeds score well under one.
scenes.caption: The score is called chi-square. Zero means a perfect match, and bigger means further off. Mendel's seeds score well under one.
scenes.visual: The sum resolves to 'χ² = 0.47' in WHITE. A horizontal number line slides in beneath, marked 0 to 12. A WHITE marker labelled 'Mendel 0.47' rests near its left end; the label '0 = perfect match' sits at zero.
scenes.narration: The score is called chi-square. Zero means a perfect match, and bigger means further off. Mendel's seeds score well under one.

scenes.tts: But is that small? We need to know what chance alone produces. So assume the ratio is true. Let a computer grow Mendel's cross thousands of times, and score every run.
scenes.visual: Mendel's marker dims to an outline. The label 'simulation: 9:3:3:1 true, 556 seeds per run' appears top left. Chapter 1's grey simulated bars flicker through runs at the top of the frame, and each run's score is computed beside it (real multinomial draws, n = 556).
scenes.narration: But is that small? We need to know what chance alone produces. So assume the ratio is true. Let a computer grow Mendel's cross thousands of times, and score every run.

scenes.tts: Each run drops one dot on this line, at its kai-square score. Where will the pile of dots balance?
scenes.caption: Each run drops one dot on this line, at its chi-square score. Where will the pile of dots balance?
scenes.visual: The first twenty runs each drop a GREY dot onto the number line, stacking where they land. A question card appears: 'Where will the pile balance?'
scenes.narration: Each run drops one dot on this line, at its chi-square score. Where will the pile of dots balance?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The question card stays; the twenty dots hold still on the line. A 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: It balances at three, not four. Each class adds a little less than one, on average. Four classes share one total. Once three counts are known, the fourth is fixed. So only three misses are free. Three is the degrees of freedom.
scenes.visual: Card dissolves. Dots rain fast until the pile holds 10,000 runs, drawn as a histogram of real simulated values (mean 3.0, right-skewed, long tail to the right). A WHITE balance triangle slides under the pile at 3 with the label 'average = 3 = degrees of freedom'. Beside it, four class boxes: three glow 'free', the fourth locks with a padlock labelled 'set by the total'.
scenes.narration: It balances at three, not four. Each class adds a little less than one, on average. Four classes share one total. Once three counts are known, the fourth is fixed. So only three misses are free. Three is the degrees of freedom.

scenes.tts: Now mark the far edge. Only one run in twenty scores beyond this line. Counts out here would be rare if the ratio held. That is a reason to doubt the ratio.
scenes.visual: A vertical WHITE line drops at 7.81, labelled '7.81'. The part of the pile to its right shades GREY-RED with the label '5% of chance runs'. The left part stays grey.
scenes.narration: Now mark the far edge. Only one run in twenty scores beyond this line. Counts out here would be rare if the ratio held. That is a reason to doubt the ratio.

scenes.visual: Silent hold. The shaded 5% tail glows softly; the rest of the pile is still.

scenes.tts: Now drop Mendel's score onto the pile. It sits far to the left, deep inside the pile. Most chance runs land further out than his did. That share of runs is called the p-value.
scenes.visual: The tail shading fades. Mendel's WHITE marker drops back in at 0.47. Everything in the pile to the right of it shades WHITE, with the label '93% of runs land further out', then 'p ≈ 0.93'.
scenes.narration: Now drop Mendel's score onto the pile. It sits far to the left, deep inside the pile. Most chance runs land further out than his did. That share of runs is called the p-value.

scenes.tts: Read it carefully. The p-value is worked out as if the ratio, and every other assumption, were true. That means independent seeds, correct scoring and equal survival. It is not the chance that the ratio is true.
scenes.visual: A card: 'p = share of chance runs at least this far off, if the ratio and every assumption hold.' Below it, a second line, 'the chance the ratio is true', appears and is struck through with a single line.
scenes.narration: Read it carefully. The p-value is worked out as if the ratio, and every other assumption, were true. That means independent seeds, correct scoring and equal survival. It is not the chance that the ratio is true.

scenes.tts: And a large p-value does not prove the ratio. It gives no reason to reject the ratio. Other models might fit these counts just as well.
scenes.visual: The struck-through line fades. A stamp reading 'not rejected' lands on the card; a second stamp 'proven' starts to land, stops in mid-air and fades out.
scenes.narration: And a large p-value does not prove the ratio. It gives no reason to reject the ratio. Other models might fit these counts just as well.

scenes.tts: So here is the idea. A ratio predicts a spread of counts. If the ratio holds, kai-square averages its degrees of freedom. Far above that, doubt the ratio, but never call it proof.
scenes.caption: So here is the idea. A ratio predicts a spread of counts. If the ratio holds, chi-square averages its degrees of freedom. Far above that, doubt the ratio, but never call it proof.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the full pile with its balance point at 3 and the shaded 5% tail beyond 7.81. The sentences appear one at a time at the top left in WHITE.
scenes.narration: So here is the idea. A ratio predicts a spread of counts. If the ratio holds, chi-square averages its degrees of freedom. Far above that, doubt the ratio, but never call it proof.

scenes.visual: End card over the dimmed pile, large white text, centred: 'Chi-square far above its degrees of freedom casts doubt on the ratio.'
